p: Swete prints "with her hair let down"; his footnote says Codex Alexandrinus has "the wars let loose."

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935). Swete's footnote gives no reading of Codex Venetus here
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete in his footnote

why: Loosened hair is the sign of a woman in mourning or pleading, and it fits the tears and wailing beside it. "The wars" (polemous) makes no sense with "let loose" said of a woman begging her troops. Here Swete's printed text is not the codex: he did not follow Alexandrinus.

t: The faithful God or the Most Great God?
p: Alexandrinus calls God "faithful" here; Venetus, and Rahlfs, have the book's usual title "the Most Great God."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Brenton's English ("the Greatest God")

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the base text. "Most Great God" is the book's stock title (1:16; 3:11), so a copyist could easily have brought it in here; but the same habit could have pushed a copyist the other way, and Rahlfs chose it. The meaning of the scene is the same either way.

p: Alexandrinus says the king was struck by the place's godliness; Venetus and Rahlfs say by its splendor.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)

why: The two Greek words differ by a few letters (eusebeia, euprepeia). Both make sense: the king admires the worship he sees, or the look of the building. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

t: Not even Gentiles, or not even Jews?
p: Alexandrinus says no Gentile may enter; Venetus and Rahlfs say no one "of the nation," that is, no Jew.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: because not even the nations (may) enter

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes ("of the nation"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935) (adds "is allowed"); Brenton ("none of the nation"); Emmet's translation (1913) follows it
readings.orig: μηδὲ τοῖς ἐκ τοῦ ἔθνους ἐξεῖναι εἰσιέναι
readings.en: because not even those of the nation are allowed to enter
readings.plain: No one of our nation may go in

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the base text, but the other reading may well be older: on that reading the answer is that not even Jews, and not all the priests, may enter, so how much less a Gentile king. In Alexandrinus the steps run Gentiles, then priests, then the high priest.

a: why should I not go into every shrine
p: Swete's Greek has "of all"; Rahlfs reads "by all means," one letter different.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (Codex Venetus has a third form, pantes, all people, from Swete's footnotes)
readings.orig: διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν οὐχὶ πάντων εἰσελεύσεσθαι
readings.en: for what reason (should I) not enter of all
readings.plain: why should I not go into every shrine

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet's translation (1913, "why should I not enter in any case")
readings.orig: διά τινα αἰτίαν οὐχὶ πάντως εἰσελεύσεσθαι
readings.en: for what reason (should I) not by all means enter
readings.plain: why should I not go in anyway

why: Pantōn ("of all") and pantōs ("by all means") differ by one letter. Swete's text is awkward Greek, and the Plain English Translation makes "all" refer to the shrines of 1:13. The king's point is the same either way: no one will stop him.

a: They even made the streets full of groaning
p: Alexandrinus has a small word meaning "even"; Venetus and Rahlfs have "wailing."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πού γε καὶ στεναγμῶν ἐνεμπίπλων τὰς πλατείας
readings.en: and indeed they filled the streets with groans
readings.plain: They even made the streets full of groaning

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet's apparatus (1913) adds cursives 44, 55, 74 and the Armenian
readings.orig: γόου τε καὶ στεναγμῶν ἐνεπίμπλων τὰς πλατείας
readings.en: and they filled the streets with wailing and groans
readings.plain: They made the streets full of wailing and groaning

why: Venetus's "wailing" pairs well with "groans," and Emmet's apparatus shows it in more witnesses, but the base text is readable, so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: left behind the bridal rooms made ready for the wedding
p: Alexandrinus and Venetus have no noun here; Rahlfs and Emmet print "the bridal chambers made ready for the meeting." The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); C. W. Emmet's text (1913), which defends the noun from the parallel in 4:6
readings.en: the bridal chambers made ready for the meeting
readings.plain: left behind the bridal rooms made ready for the wedding

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, and cursive 55, from Emmet's apparatus; Swete prints this reading, but his footnote shows that Alexandrinus itself ends the last word in the feminine singular (διατεταγμενην (sic) A, where the digital text breaks the word across a line), so his masculine plural is his own correction
readings.en: those (masculine) now made ready for everything
readings.plain: left behind everything now made ready

why: In Swete's Greek the article "those" is masculine but has no noun with it, which suggests a word has dropped out. Emmet notes that the bridal room of 4:6 confirms pastous, and that Alexandrinus's feminine ending suggests apantēsin ("meeting") stood in the original. This is a departure from the base text.

p: Venetus and Rahlfs add "in the city"; Alexandrinus says only that they ran in disorder. Goes with the variant before it.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.en: a disorderly race in the city

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete

why: The Plain English Translation follows Rahlfs's text through this verse (see the variant on the wedding rooms). The words add nothing the scene does not already imply.

t: By the law, or for the law?
p: Swete's Greek has "under" the ancestral law; Rahlfs prints "for" it.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (A; Swete's footnotes record no difference in V here)
Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.en: on behalf of the ancestral law

why: Hypo ("under, by") and hyper ("for") are easily confused. "For the law" is the usual phrase for martyrs (2 Maccabees 7:9), and Rahlfs adopts it. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text, which can mean dying as the law requires.

a: So the high priest Simon knelt down, facing the sanctuary. He held his hands out in an orderly way and prayed like this:
t: A verse not in Alexandrinus or Venetus
p: Swete's text, Alexandrinus and Venetus have no verse 2:1; the Lucianic text has it. The Plain English Translation gives it in brackets.

readings.w: The Lucianic text, a group of later manuscripts (NETS's introduction); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935). NETS keeps it in square brackets; Brenton's English has it
readings.orig: ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀρχιερεὺς Σιμων ἐξ ἐναντίας τοῦ ναοῦ κάμψας τὰ γόνατα καὶ τὰς χεῖρας προτείνας εὐτάκτως ἐποιήσατο τὴν δέησιν τοιαύτην
readings.en: So the high priest Simon, facing the sanctuary, bending his knees and stretching out his hands in good order, made a prayer like this
readings.plain: So the high priest Simon knelt down, facing the sanctuary. He held his hands out in an orderly way and prayed like this:

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus (NETS's introduction; Emmet's apparatus adds cursives 55 and 71); Swete's printed text, whose footnotes say nothing at 2:1; Hanhart's Göttingen edition (1980) leaves it out, as NETS's footnote says
Cursives 44 and 74, from Emmet's apparatus
readings.en: and they said with one accord

why: The textual evidence is against the verse: it is missing from both great codices, and NETS's translator, Cameron Boyd-Taylor, says it "is most readily explained as an addition." But without it the prayer of 2:2-20 has no speaker, and 2:21 speaks of "the prayer" as offered rightly. Boyd-Taylor kept it for that literary reason, in square brackets, and the Plain English Translation does the same.
b: Emmet's apparatus also reports that the Armenian version has "they began to pray and said." The Greek here is quoted from Rahlfs's edition. The Plain English Translation's brackets mark a verse that is not in the base text.

p: Alexandrinus has "weakness" where Swete prints "power"; Swete corrected the codex.

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
Codex Alexandrinus, from Swete's footnote ("σθενει] ασθενει (sic) A")

why: Asthenei ("weakness") is one letter longer than sthenei ("strength") and makes no sense of a proud king. Here Swete's printed text is not the codex.

a: their wicked ways were plain for all to see
p: Alexandrinus says the Sodomites became "unseen" in their wickedness; Venetus and Rahlfs say "conspicuous." The Plain English Translation follows Venetus.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes ("διαδηλους V vid," that is, as far as the page can be read); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet's translation (1913, "known of all"); Brenton ("notorious")
readings.en: having become conspicuous in their vices
readings.plain: their wicked ways were plain for all to see

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (Swete's text)
readings.en: having become unseen (obscure) in their vices
readings.plain: their wicked ways were hidden from sight

why: The two words differ only by the letters di-. "Hidden" does not fit a city whose sin is the byword of the Bible (Genesis 18:20; Ezekiel 16:49), and "conspicuous" sets up "an example to later generations." This is a departure from the base text.

a: made your power known. By them you made your great might known.
p: Venetus lacks the words "your power ... you made known," so its Pharaoh line says it once.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet's apparatus adds the Armenian and most cursives
readings.orig: ἐγνώρισας τὴν σὴν δύναμιν, ἐφ᾽ αἷς ἐγνώρισας τὸ μέγα σου κράτος
readings.en: you made known your power, by which you made known your great might
readings.plain: made your power known. By them you made your great might known.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Brenton's English agrees
readings.en: you made known your great might

why: Venetus's copyist may have skipped from the first "you made known" to the second. Emmet (1913) took the longer text instead as a probable conflation of two readings. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

p: Alexandrinus says "our place"; Rahlfs prints "this place."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Brenton ("this house")

why: Simon is praying in the temple, so "this place" fits, as in 2:9, 14 and 16; but "our place" is the base text and means the same temple.

p: Swete's Greek has no "us"; Rahlfs and the Greek of Psalm 78:8, which this line quotes, have it.

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); the Septuagint of Psalm 78:8 (Psalm 79:8 in English), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ταχὺ προκαταλαβέτωσαν ἡμᾶς οἱ οἰκτιρμοί σου
readings.en: let your mercies quickly come to meet us

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus); Swete's footnotes give no other reading of V here
readings.en: let your mercies be quick to come first

why: The verb needs an object in English, and the line is a quotation of Psalm 78:8 in the Septuagint, which has "us." This is a small departure from the base text.

p: Alexandrinus and Venetus both say "others"; Swete and Rahlfs print "companions," a one-letter change.

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnotes

why: Hetairōn ("companions") and heterōn ("others") differ by one letter. "Drinking partners and companions" is a natural pair; "drinking partners and others" is weak. Here Swete's printed text is not the codex: he corrected both manuscripts.

a: the mark of Dionysus, an ivy leaf
p: Both codices have "for Dionysus" (dative); Swete prints "of Dionysus" (genitive).

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.en: with the ivy-leaf emblem of Dionysus
readings.plain: the mark of Dionysus, an ivy leaf

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnote ("Διονυσω AV")
readings.en: with an ivy-leaf emblem for Dionysus
readings.plain: a mark for Dionysus, an ivy leaf

why: Swete's genitive is his own correction of both codices. The meaning hardly changes: the brand is the god's emblem either way, and the Plain English Translation's wording would fit both.
b: Swete's footnotes record more in this verse. Venetus seems to read "and Sophyllus" for "ivy leaf" ("κισσοφυλλω] και Σοφυλλω Vvid"), a copying slip. For "to be listed" Swete prints prokatachōrisai ("to be listed beforehand"), as Alexandrinus has; Venetus has katachōrēsai ("προκαταχωρισαι] καταχωρησαι V"), and Rahlfs prints katachōrisai, "to be listed," without "beforehand." The Plain English Translation's "already set" belongs to the next word, which all of them share.

a: Some gave themselves up readily and lightly
p: Venetus first wrote "over the city"; its corrector and Swete have "lightly." Brenton follows the first.

readings.w: Swete's printed text; the corrector of Codex Venetus; Codex Alexandrinus in another spelling ("επιπολειως A"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.plain: Some gave themselves up readily and lightly

readings.w: The first hand of Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnote ("επι πολεως V* (επιπολαιως Vᵃ)"); Brenton ("Some of those who were over the city")
readings.plain: Some of those over the city gave themselves up readily

why: Epipolaiōs ("on the surface, lightly") and epi poleōs ("over the city") sound almost the same. Emmet (1913) keeps "lightly" as the best attested reading and takes it as "obviously." See the note on the next words.

t: Hateful to some, or some hateful?
p: Emmet and Rahlfs read "they seemed hateful to some"; Alexandrinus, which Swete prints, says "some seemed hateful." The Plain English Translation follows the first.

readings.w: C. W. Emmet's text (1913) and Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Brenton ("some persons held them in odium")
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), printed by Swete; Emmet's apparatus names A for this reading, and Swete's footnotes give no other reading of V
readings.plain: some of them came to be seen as hateful

why: The two differ by one letter (enioi, eniois), but the subject changes. On Alexandrinus's reading the narrator says some Jews were hateful and then at once that everyone thought well of them (3:5-6). The dative limits the hatred to some outsiders, which is what the next verses say. This is a departure from the base text.

p: Alexandrinus has a word meaning "ruin"; Swete prints "in the matter of food," as Venetus has.

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Codex Venetus and cursives 62 and 64, from Emmet's apparatus; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
Codex Alexandrinus, from Swete's footnote ("καταστροφας A") and Emmet's apparatus

why: Kata tas trophas ("as to foods") and katastrophas ("overthrow") are the same letters run together. Only "food" makes sense with 3:7, where the Jews keep apart in worship and food. Here Swete's printed text is not the codex.

p: Alexandrinus says the slanderers pinned "no small fear" on the Jews; Venetus and Rahlfs say "no small blame."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet ("no small opprobrium"); Brenton ("much odium")

why: Phobos ("fear") and psogos ("blame") look alike in Greek capitals. "Blame" suits slander better; "fear" makes the Jews into a feared threat, which is the point of 3:7. The base text is kept.

a: we were glad to be good to them
p: Both codices read a phrase that makes no sense here; Swete and Rahlfs print "gladly."

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.plain: we were glad to be good to them

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnotes

why: Asmenōs ("gladly") makes sense; men hōs ("indeed as") breaks the sentence, and the two share most of their letters. Swete's printed text is not the codex here.

a: We were also led up to Jerusalem
p: Venetus and Rahlfs have a verb meaning "we were moved" (to go up); Alexandrinus has "we were brought."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: We were also led up to Jerusalem

readings.w: Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnote ("προηχθημεν V"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)
readings.plain: We were also moved to go up to Jerusalem

why: The verbs differ by one letter. Either way the king presents his visit as an act of honor; the Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: to make them partners with our priests for all time
t: Our priests, our rites, or nothing
p: Alexandrinus says "partners with the priests"; Rahlfs reads "sharers in the rites"; Venetus lacks the words.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: to make them partners with our priests for all time

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935); Emmet reports that earlier editors translate "eternal religious rites"; Brenton ("the everlasting rites of our solemnities")
readings.plain: to make them sharers in our rites for all time

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes ("om και μετοχους…καταστησαι V"); Emmet's apparatus adds cursives 62 and 64 and the Armenian

why: Hiereōn ("priests") and hierōn ("rites, sacred things") differ by one letter. Either way the offer is to draw the Jews into the king's own cult, the same bargain as 2:30. The base text is kept.

p: Alexandrinus says "most hateful" tortures; Venetus and Rahlfs say "most shameful."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnote ("εχθισταις] αισχισταις V"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)

why: The two words look much alike. Both make the same threat; the Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

t: The royal treasury or the royal silver
p: Venetus and Rahlfs say "from the royal silver"; Alexandrinus says "from the royal (treasury)."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnote ("βασιλειον] βασιλικου αργυριου V"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935)

why: The sense is the same: the king pays the informer from his own funds. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.
